{{Short description|Description in Riemannian geometry}}
In [[Riemannian geometry]], the '''sectional curvature''' is one of the ways to describe the [[curvature of Riemannian manifolds]]. The sectional curvature <math>K(\sigma_p)</math> depends on a two-dimensional linear subspace <math>\sigma_p</math> of the [[tangent space]] at a point <math>p</math> of the manifold. It can be defined geometrically as the [[Gaussian curvature]] of the [[surface (topology)|surface]] which has the plane <math>\sigma_p</math> as a tangent plane at <math>p</math>, obtained from [[geodesic]]s which start at <math>p</math> in the directions of <math>\sigma_p</math> (in other words, the image of <math>\sigma_p</math> under the [[exponential map (Riemannian geometry)|exponential map]] at <math>p</math>). The sectional curvature is a real-valued function on the 2-[[Grassmannian]] [[fiber bundle|bundle]] over the manifold.

The sectional curvature determines the [[Riemann curvature tensor]] completely.

== Definition ==
Given a [[Riemannian manifold]] and two [[linearly independent]] [[tangent vectors]] at the same point, ''u'' and ''v'', we can define
: <math>K(u,v)={\langle R(u,v)v,u\rangle\over \langle u,u\rangle\langle v,v\rangle-\langle u,v\rangle^2}</math>

Here ''R'' is the [[Riemann curvature tensor]], defined here by the convention {{tmath|1= R(u,v)w=\nabla_u\nabla_vw-\nabla_v\nabla_uw-\nabla_{[u,v]}w }}. Some sources use the opposite convention {{tmath|1= R(u,v)w=\nabla_v\nabla_uw-\nabla_u\nabla_vw-\nabla_{[v,u]}w }}, in which case <math>K(u,v)</math> must be defined with <math>\langle R(u,v)u,v\rangle</math> in the numerator instead of <math>\langle R(u,v)v,u\rangle.</math>{{sfnm|1a1=Gallot|1a2=Hulin|1a3=Lafontaine|1y=2004|1loc=Section 3.A.2}}

Note that the linear independence of ''u'' and ''v'' forces the denominator in the above expression to be nonzero, so that {{nowrap|''K''(''u'', ''v'')}} is well-defined. In particular, if ''u'' and ''v'' are [[orthonormal]], then the definition takes on the simple form
: <math>K(u,v) = \langle R(u,v)v,u\rangle.</math>
It is straightforward to check that if <math>u,v\in T_pM</math> are linearly independent and span the same two-dimensional linear subspace of the [[tangent space]] <math>T_pM</math> as {{tmath| x,y\in T_pM }}, then {{tmath|1= K(u,v)=K(x,y) }}. So one may consider the sectional curvature as a real-valued function whose input is a two-dimensional linear subspace of a tangent space.

=== Alternative definitions ===
Alternatively, the sectional curvature can be characterized by the circumference of small circles. Let <math>P</math> be a two-dimensional plane in {{tmath| T_xM }}. Let <math>C_P(r)</math> for sufficiently small <math>r > 0</math> denote the image under the exponential map at <math>p</math> of the unit circle in {{tmath| P }}, and let <math>l_P(r)</math> denote the length of {{tmath| C_P(r) }}. Then it can be proven that
: <math>l_P(r)=2\pi r \left(1-{r^2\over 6}\sigma(P)+O(r^3)\right),</math>
as {{tmath| r \to 0 }}, for some number {{tmath| \sigma(P) }}. This number <math>\sigma(P)</math> at <math>p</math> is the sectional curvature of <math>P</math> at {{tmath| p }}.{{sfnm|1a1=Gallot|1a2=Hulin|1a3=Lafontaine|1y=2004|1loc=Section 3.D.4}}

== Manifolds with constant sectional curvature ==
One says that a Riemannian manifold has "constant curvature {{tmath| \kappa }}" if <math>\operatorname{sec}(P)=\kappa</math> for all two-dimensional linear subspaces <math>P\subset T_pM</math> and for all {{tmath| p\in M }}.

The [[Schur's lemma (Riemannian geometry)|Schur lemma]] states that if {{nowrap|(''M'', ''g'')}} is a connected Riemannian manifold with dimension at least three, and if there is a function <math>f:M\to\mathbb{R}</math> such that <math>\operatorname{sec}(P)=f(p)</math> for all two-dimensional linear subspaces <math>P\subset T_pM</math> and for all {{tmath| p\in M }}, then ''f'' must be constant and hence {{nowrap|(''M'', ''g'')}} has constant curvature.

A Riemannian manifold with constant sectional curvature is called a [[space form]]. If <math>\kappa</math> denotes the constant value of the sectional curvature, then the curvature tensor can be written as
: <math>R(u,v)w=\kappa \big(\langle v,w\rangle u-\langle u,w\rangle v\big)</math>
for any {{tmath| u,v,w\in T_pM }}.
{| role="presentation" class="wikitable mw-collapsible mw-collapsed"
| style="font-weight:bold;' | Proof
|-
| Briefly: one polarization argument gives a formula for <math>R(u,v)v,</math> a second (equivalent) polarization argument gives a formula for <math>R(u,v)w+R(u,w)v,</math> and a combination with the first Bianchi identity recovers the given formula for <math>R(u,v)w.</math>

From the definition of sectional curvature, we know that <math>\langle R(u, v)v, u\rangle = \kappa\left(|u|^2|v|^2 - \langle u, v \rangle^2\right)</math> whenever <math>u,v</math> are linearly independent, and this easily extends to the case that <math>u,v</math> are linearly dependent since both sides are then zero. Now, given arbitrary ''u,v,w,'' compute <math>\langle R(u+w,v)v,u+w\rangle</math> in two ways. First, according to the above formula, it equals
: <math>\kappa\left(|v|^2\left(|u|^2 + |w|^2 + 2\langle u, w \rangle\right) - \langle u, v \rangle^2 - \langle w, v \rangle^2 - 2\langle u, v \rangle\langle w, v \rangle\right).</math>

Secondly, by multilinearity, it equals <math>\langle R(u,v)v,u\rangle+\langle R(w,v)v,w\rangle+\langle R(u,v)v,w\rangle+\langle R(w,v)v,u\rangle,</math>

which, recalling the Riemannian symmetry <math>\langle R(u,v)v,w\rangle=\langle R(w,v)v,u\rangle,</math> can be simplified to
: <math>\kappa\Big(|u|^2|v|^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2\Big)+\kappa\Big(|w|^2|v|^2-\langle w,v\rangle^2\Big)+2\langle R(u,v)v,w\rangle.</math>

Setting these two computations equal to each other and canceling terms, one finds
: <math>\langle R(u,v)v,w\rangle = \kappa\Big(|v|^2\langle u,w\rangle - \langle u,v\rangle\langle w,v\rangle\Big).</math>

Since ''w'' is arbitrary this shows that
: <math>R(u,v)v=\kappa\Big(|v|^2u-\langle u,v\rangle v\Big)</math>

for any ''u,v.'' Now let ''u,v,w'' be arbitrary and compute <math>R(u,v+w)(v+w)</math> in two ways. Firstly, by this new formula, it equals
: <math>\kappa\left(\left(|v|^2 + |w|^2 + 2\langle v, w \rangle\right)u - \langle u, v \rangle v - \langle u, w \rangle v - \langle u, v \rangle w - \langle u, w \rangle w\right).</math>

Secondly, by multilinearity, it equals <math>R(u,v)v+R(u,w)w+R(u,v)w+R(u,w)v</math> which by the new formula equals
: <math>\kappa\left(|v|^2u - \langle u, v \rangle v\right) + \kappa\left(|w|^2u - \langle u, w \rangle w\right) + R(u, v)w + R(u, w)v.</math>

Setting these two computations equal to each other shows
: <math>R(u, v)w + R(u, w)v = \kappa\left(2\langle v, w \rangle u - \langle u, w \rangle v - \langle u, v \rangle w\right).</math>

Swap <math>u</math> and <math>v</math>, then add this to the Bianchi identity <math>R(v, u)w + R(u, w)v + R(w, v)u = 0</math> to get
: <math>2R(v, u)w + R(u, w)v = \kappa\left(2\langle u, w \rangle v - \langle v, w \rangle u - \langle u, v \rangle w\right).</math>

Subtract these two equations, making use of the symmetry <math>R(u, v)w = -R(v, u)w,</math> to get
: <math>3R(u, v)w = 3\kappa\left(\langle v, w \rangle u - \langle u, w \rangle v\right).</math>
|}

Since any Riemannian metric is parallel with respect to its Levi-Civita connection, this shows that the Riemann tensor of any constant-curvature space is also parallel. The Ricci tensor is then given by <math>\operatorname{Ric} = (n - 1)\kappa g</math> and the scalar curvature is <math>n(n - 1)\kappa.</math> In particular, any constant-curvature space is Einstein and has constant scalar curvature.

=== Model examples ===

Given a positive number <math>a,</math> define
* <math>\left(\mathbb{R}^n, g_{\mathbb{R}^n}\right)</math> to be the standard Riemannian structure
* <math>\left(S^n(a), g_{S^n(a)}\right)</math> to be the sphere <math>S^n(a) \equiv \left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}: |x| = a\right\}</math> with <math>g_{S^n(a)}</math> given by the pullback of the standard Riemannian structure on <math>\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math> by the inclusion map <math>S^n(a) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math>
* <math>\left(H^n(a), g_{H^n(a)}\right)</math> to be the ball <math>H^n(a) \equiv \left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: |x| < a\right\}</math> with <math>g_{H^n(a)} = a^2\frac{\bigl(a^2 - |x|{}^2\bigr)\left(dx_1^2 + \cdots + dx_n^2\right) - \left(x_1 dx_1 + \cdots + x_n dx_n\right)^2}{\bigl(a^2 - |x|{}^2\bigr)^2}.</math>
In the usual terminology, these Riemannian manifolds are referred to as [[Euclidean space]], the [[n-sphere|''n''-sphere]], and [[hyperbolic space]]. Here, the point is that each is a complete connected smooth Riemannian manifold with constant curvature. To be precise, the Riemannian metric <math>g_{\mathbb{R}^n}</math> has constant curvature 0, the Riemannian metric <math>g_{S^n(a)}</math> has constant curvature {{tmath| 1/a^2 }}, and the Riemannian metric <math>g_{H^n(a)}</math> has constant curvature {{tmath| -1/a^2 }}.

Furthermore, these are the 'universal' examples in the sense that if <math>(M, g)</math> is a smooth, connected, and simply-connected complete Riemannian manifold with constant curvature, then it is isometric to one of the above examples; the particular example is dictated by the value of the constant curvature of <math>g,</math> according to the constant curvatures of the above examples.

If <math>(M, g)</math> is a smooth and connected complete Riemannian manifold with constant curvature, but is ''not'' assumed to be simply-connected, then consider the universal covering space <math>\pi:\widetilde{M}\to M</math> with the pullback Riemannian metric {{tmath| \pi^\ast g }}. Since <math>\pi</math> is, by topological principles, a covering map, the Riemannian manifold <math>(\widetilde{M},\pi^\ast g)</math> is locally isometric to {{tmath| (M,g) }}, and so it is a smooth, connected, and simply-connected complete Riemannian manifold with the same constant curvature as {{tmath| g }}. It must then be isometric one of the above model examples. Note that the deck transformations of the universal cover are [[isometry|isometries]] relative to the metric {{tmath| \pi^\ast g }}.

The study of Riemannian manifolds with constant negative curvature is called [[hyperbolic geometry]].

== Scaling ==
Let <math>(M, g)</math> be a smooth manifold, and let <math>\lambda</math> be a positive number. Consider the Riemannian manifold {{tmath| (M, \lambda g) }}. The curvature tensor, as a multilinear map <math>T_pM\times T_pM\times T_pM\to T_pM,</math> is unchanged by this modification. Let <math>v,w</math> be linearly independent vectors in {{tmath| T_pM }}. Then
: <math>K_{\lambda g}(v, w) = \frac{\lambda g\left(R^{\lambda g}(v, w)w, v\right)}{|v|_{\lambda g}^2|w|_{\lambda g}^2 - \langle v, w \rangle\vphantom|_{\lambda g}^2} = \frac{1}{\lambda}\frac{g\left(R^g(v, w)w, v\right)}{|v|_g^2|w|_g^2 - \langle v, w \rangle\vphantom|_g^2} = \frac{1}{\lambda}K_g(v,w).</math>
So multiplication of the metric by <math>\lambda</math> multiplies all of the sectional curvatures by {{tmath| \lambda^{-1} }}.

== Toponogov's theorem ==
[[Toponogov's theorem]] affords a characterization of sectional curvature in terms of how "fat" [[geodesic triangle]]s appear when compared to their Euclidean counterparts.  The basic intuition is that, if a space is positively curved, then the edge of a triangle opposite some given vertex will tend to bend away from that vertex, whereas if a space is negatively curved, then the opposite edge of the triangle will tend to bend towards the vertex.

More precisely, let ''M'' be a [[complete space|complete]] Riemannian manifold, and let ''xyz'' be a geodesic triangle in ''M'' (a triangle each of whose sides is a length-minimizing geodesic).  Finally, let ''m'' be the midpoint of the geodesic ''xy''.  If ''M'' has non-negative curvature, then for all sufficiently small triangles
: <math>d(z,m)^2 \ge \tfrac12 d(z,x)^2 + \tfrac12 d(z,y)^2 - \tfrac14 d(x,y)^2</math>
where ''d'' is the [[distance function]] on ''M''.  The case of equality holds precisely when the curvature of ''M'' vanishes, and the right-hand side represents the distance from a vertex to the opposite side of a geodesic triangle in Euclidean space having the same side-lengths as the triangle ''xyz''.  This makes precise the sense in which triangles are "fatter" in positively curved spaces.  In non-positively curved spaces, the inequality goes the other way:
: <math>d(z,m)^2 \le \tfrac12 d(z,x)^2 + \tfrac12 d(z,y)^2 - \tfrac14 d(x,y)^2.</math>

If tighter bounds on the sectional curvature are known, then this property generalizes to give a [[comparison theorem]] between geodesic triangles in ''M'' and those in a suitable simply connected space form; see [[Toponogov's theorem]].  Simple consequences of the version stated here are:
* A complete Riemannian manifold has non-negative sectional curvature if and only if the function <math>f_p(x) = \operatorname{dist}^2(p,x)</math> is 1-[[Glossary of Riemannian and metric geometry|concave]] for all points ''p''.
* A complete simply connected Riemannian manifold has non-positive sectional curvature if and only if the function <math>f_p(x) = \operatorname{dist}^2(p,x)</math> is 1-[[Glossary of Riemannian and metric geometry|convex]].

== Manifolds with non-positive sectional curvature ==
In 1928, [[Élie Cartan]] proved the [[Cartan–Hadamard theorem]]: if ''M'' is a [[Complete space|complete]] manifold with non-positive sectional curvature, then its [[universal cover]] is [[diffeomorphic]] to a [[Euclidean space]]. In particular, it is [[Aspherical space|aspherical]]: the [[homotopy groups]] <math>\pi_i(M)</math> for ''i'' &ge; 2 are trivial.  Therefore, the topological structure of a complete non-positively curved manifold is determined by its [[fundamental group]]. [[Preissman's theorem]] restricts the fundamental group of negatively curved compact manifolds. The [[Cartan–Hadamard conjecture]] states that the classical [[isoperimetric inequality]] should hold in all simply connected spaces of non-positive curvature, which are called [[Hadamard manifold|Cartan–Hadamard manifolds]].

== Manifolds with positive sectional curvature ==
Little is known about the structure of positively curved manifolds. The [[soul theorem]] ({{harvnb|Cheeger|Gromoll|1972}}; {{harvnb|Gromoll|Meyer|1969}}) implies that a complete non-compact non-negatively curved manifold is diffeomorphic to a normal bundle over a compact non-negatively curved manifold. As for compact positively curved manifolds, there are two classical results:
* It follows from the [[Myers theorem]] that the fundamental group of such a manifold is finite.
* It follows from the [[Synge theorem]] that the fundamental group of such a manifold in even dimensions is 0, if orientable and <math>\mathbb Z_2</math> otherwise. In odd dimensions a positively curved manifold is always orientable.

Moreover, there are relatively few examples of compact positively curved manifolds, leaving a lot of conjectures (e.g., the [[Hopf conjecture]] on whether there is a metric of positive sectional curvature on {{tmath| \mathbb S^2 \times \mathbb S^2 }}). The most typical way of constructing new examples is the following corollary from the O'Neill curvature formulas: if <math>(M, g)</math> is a Riemannian manifold admitting a free isometric action of a Lie group G, and M has positive sectional curvature on all 2-planes orthogonal to the orbits of G, then the manifold <math>M/G</math> with the quotient metric has positive sectional curvature. This fact allows one to construct the classical positively curved spaces, being spheres and projective spaces, as well as these examples {{harv|Ziller|2007}}:
* The Berger spaces <math>B^7=\operatorname{SO}(5)/\operatorname{SO}(3)</math> and {{tmath|1= B^{13}=\operatorname{SU}(5)/\operatorname{Sp}(2) \cdot \mathbb S^1 }}.
* The Wallach spaces (or the homogeneous flag manifolds): <math>W^6=\operatorname{SU}(3)/T^2</math>, <math>W^{12}=\operatorname{Sp}(3)/\operatorname{Sp}(1)^3</math> and <math>W^{24}=F_4/\operatorname{Spin}(8)</math>.
* The Aloff–Wallach spaces <math>W^7_{p,q} = \operatorname{SU}(3)/\operatorname{diag}\left(z^p, z^q, \overline{z}^{p+q}\right)</math>.
* The Eschenburg spaces <math>E_{k,l} = \operatorname{diag}\left(z^{k_1}, z^{k_2}, z^{k_3}\right)\backslash \operatorname{SU}(3)/\operatorname{diag}\left(z^{l_1}, z^{l_2}, z^{l_3}\right)^{-1}.</math>
* The Bazaikin spaces <math>B^{13}_p = \operatorname{diag}\left(z_1^{p_1}, \dots, z_1^{p_5}\right)\backslash \operatorname{U}(5)/\operatorname{diag}(z_2 A, 1)^{-1}</math>, where <math>A\in \operatorname{Sp}(2)\subset \operatorname{SU}(4)</math>.

== Manifolds with non-negative sectional curvature ==
Cheeger and Gromoll proved their soul theorem which states that any non-negatively curved complete non-compact manifold <math>M</math> has a totally convex compact submanifold <math>S</math> such that <math>M</math> is diffeomorphic to the normal bundle of {{tmath| S }}. Such an <math>S</math> is called the soul of {{tmath| M }}. In particular, this theorem implies that <math>M</math> is homotopic to its soul <math>S</math> which has the dimension less than <math>M</math>.
